questions.q: A 2-week-old term neonate presents with multiple 1–2 mm yellow papules clustered over the nose, cheeks, and forehead. The mother is concerned these represent infection. Histology shows enlarged sebaceous lobules with lipid-laden sebocytes surrounding a dilated follicular ostium. What is the most likely diagnosis and primary management?
opts: Neonatal cephalic pustulosis; topical antifungal therapy
Neonatal sebaceous gland hyperplasia; reassurance only
Miliaria crystallina; topical corticosteroid
Milia; manual extraction of keratin cysts
questions.exp: Neonatal sebaceous gland hyperplasia is a benign physiological condition caused by transplacental maternal androgens, presenting as yellow macules/papules at the follicular ostia on the central face. The condition resolves spontaneously by 4–6 months as maternal androgens are cleared, requiring only parental reassurance. Milia coexist in up to 40% of cases but are pearly-white firm keratin cysts, not yellow papules at the ostia.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 1] Physiological, Pigmentary and Mechanical Neonatal Lesions
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: Picture a YELLOW GRANDMA's FACE in the castle nursery (nose/cheeks), her sebaceous glands PUMPED UP by MATERNAL ANDROGENS coursing through the placental plumbing—but it all DRAINS and DEFLATES by 6 months when mom's hormones fade like footsteps down the hall.

questions.q: A 7-year-old child presents with discrete, light pink macules and papules on the face that spread caudally over 2 days. Examination reveals tender suboccipital and postauricular lymphadenopathy that preceded the rash by 4 days. Which clinical feature most distinctly differentiates this exanthem from measles?
opts: The rash coalesces extensively and persists for 7–10 days
The rash is fainter, does not coalesce as extensively, and fades rapidly within 3 days
The rash appears first on the trunk and spreads centripetally
The rash is accompanied by Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa
questions.exp: Rubella exanthem is characteristically fainter than measles, does not coalesce as extensively, and fades rapidly (often within 3 days) in the same order it appeared. In contrast, measles presents with a more confluent, longer-lasting rash and characteristic Koplik spots.

questions.q: A 1-day-old Black neonate has a large slate-blue macule over the lumbosacral region. Parents worry it is a bruise from birth trauma. Which mechanism best explains the blue-grey coloration and why this lesion will likely persist into childhood?
opts: Superficial dermal bruising from mechanical trauma; resolves as hemoglobin is reabsorbed
Ectopic dermal melanocytes entrapped during neural crest migration; deep location and Tyndall effect produce blue-grey color and persistence
Immature angiogenesis causing venous congestion; resolves as vascular development completes
Transient dermal edema compressing superficial vessels; resolves within 2–3 weeks
questions.exp: Mongolian spot (congenital dermal melanocytosis) results from incomplete neural crest migration of melanocytes, leaving them entrapped deep in the dermis. The blue-grey colour arises from the Tyndall effect: deep dermal melanin absorbs longer (red/yellow) wavelengths and reflects scattered shorter (blue/violet) wavelengths. Present in 90–100% of Asian and Black neonates, these lesions persist into childhood and may never fully resolve, distinguishing them from birth-related bruising which resolves over weeks.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 1] Physiological, Pigmentary and Mechanical Neonatal Lesions
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: Deep in the castle's DUNGEONS live MELANOCYTE PRISONERS (failed neural crest migrants) trapped in the DERMIS. A BLUE SPOTLIGHT (Tyndall) shines on them, swallowing the REDS but bouncing back BLUES—a permanent, harmless prisoner of the pigment jail.

questions.q: A 2-day-old neonate presents with a 2.5 cm × 2.8 cm dark brown macule on the left shoulder with coarse terminal hair. The lesion is expected to grow proportionately with the child. According to projected adult size classification, which category does this nevus fall into, and what is the associated melanoma risk?
opts: Small CMN; lifetime melanoma risk approaches that of acquired nevi
Medium CMN (M1); requires surveillance but low melanoma risk
Large CMN (L1); substantial lifetime melanoma risk requiring close monitoring
Giant CMN (G1); melanoma risk 10–14% requiring surgical intervention
questions.exp: The lesion measures 2.5 cm, which falls within the 1.5–10 cm range (M1 subtype of Medium CMN). Medium CMNs typically display hypertrichosis and have a moderate melanoma risk, though the risk is substantially lower than large or giant CMNs. Small CMNs (<1.5 cm) have negligible melanoma risk; this lesion exceeds that threshold. The presence of multiple medium CMNs (≥3) significantly increases neurocutaneous melanosis risk.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a child GROWING like JACK'S BEANSTALK (proportional growth) with a 2.5 cm MEDIUM HAIRY SHOULDER BADGE—not small, not giant—the Goldilocks CMN in the middle tower.

questions.q: A 5-day-old male premature infant born at 28 weeks presents with rapidly progressive, diffuse, board-like induration of the skin starting from the buttocks and thighs, with characteristic yellowish-white discoloration and purplish mottling. The infant is severely septic with peripheral circulatory collapse. Histopathology shows fat necrosis with doubly refractile, needle-shaped clefts arranged radially within adipocytes and thickened connective tissue septa, with minimal inflammation. What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism underlying this condition?
opts: Autoimmune-mediated destruction of adipocytes triggered by neonatal sepsis
Crystallization and solidification of subcutaneous fat due to high saturated fatty acid content and impaired lipolytic mobilization in the setting of circulatory collapse and hypothermia
Vasculitis of subcutaneous vessels leading to secondary adipocyte necrosis and inflammation
Infection of subcutaneous tissue by gram-negative bacteria producing lipase enzymes that digest adipose tissue
questions.exp: Sclerema neonatorum is caused by the unique biochemistry of neonatal fat, which contains a high ratio of saturated to unsaturated fatty acids (higher melting point than adult fat). In severely ill premature infants with circulatory collapse, peripheral hypothermia combined with immature enzymatic lipolytic mechanisms prevents fat mobilization, leading to rapid crystallization of triglycerides. The characteristic histological finding of doubly refractile needle-shaped clefts represents dissolved triglyceride crystals within adipocytes.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 4] Sclerema neonatorum vs Subcutaneous fat necrosis of newborn
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: In a frozen castle dungeon, premature ICE-CREAM (immature lipase) melts slowly while CRYSTALLINE NEEDLES (saturated fats) form rigidly—imagine the baby's skin becoming a SOLID SLAB as the cold temperature LOCKS the fat molecules in place like a tragic sculpture.

questions.q: A 5-year-old girl with a 3-month history of typical PLC with trunk involvement is now found to have identical lesions confined exclusively to her palms and soles bilaterally. Which variant of pityriasis lichenoides chronica is most likely being demonstrated?
opts: Classic pityriasis lichenoides chronica (Juliusberg disease)
Segmental pityriasis lichenoides chronica
Acral pityriasis lichenoides chronica
Varioliform pityriasis lichenoides chronica
questions.exp: Acral PLC is a rare morphological variant where micaceous scaly papules are strictly or predominantly isolated to palms and soles, contrasting with classic PLC which typically spares acral regions. This variant mimics palmoplantar psoriasis or secondary syphilis, requiring careful histopathological and serological evaluation to exclude other diagnoses.

questions.q: A 2-day-old neonate presents with generalized erythroderma, superficial blistering, and erosions across >90% of body surface area. Histopathology reveals pathognomonic epidermolytic hyperkeratosis with prominent vacuolar degeneration of suprabasal and granular layers, and dense clumps of keratin intermediate filaments. Which genetic defect is responsible for this condition?
opts: Mutations in ALOX12B and ALOXE3 affecting lipid processing
Mutations in KRT1 and KRT10 encoding keratin intermediate filaments
Mutations in SPINK5 gene causing loss of protease inhibition
Mutations in NIPAL4 and PNPLA1 affecting stratum corneum transport
questions.exp: Epidermolytic ichthyosis (bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma) is caused by mutations in KRT1 and KRT10 genes, which encode keratin intermediate filaments in the suprabasal layers. The pathognomonic histological finding is epidermolytic hyperkeratosis with vacuolar degeneration and keratin clumping. The other mutations correspond to different ichthyosis types: ALOX12B/ALOXE3 in CIE, SPINK5 in Netherton syndrome, and NIPAL4/PNPLA1 in ARCI spectrum disorders.
questions.memory_aid: 🏰 Palace: Picture a KERATINOUS KNIGHT (KRT1/KRT10) standing in the SPINOUS TOWER (suprabasal layer), his armor CRUMBLING into CLUMPS of intermediate filaments—the castle is literally collapsing from within with BLISTERS forming as the castle foundation fails.

questions.q: A 4-year-old with congenital autosomal recessive hair fragility undergoes polarizing light microscopy showing alternating bright and dark bands across the hair shaft (tiger-tail pattern), combined with short stature, intellectual impairment, ichthyosis, and photosensitivity. A deficiency in sulfur-containing amino acids (cysteine/cystine) is suspected. Which genetic complex is most likely mutated?
opts: Argininosuccinate lyase (associated with argininosuccinic aciduria)
TFIIH complex genes including ERCC2/XPD, ERCC3/XPB, or GTF2H5/TTDA
Inner root sheath keratogenous zone proteins
Copper-transporting ATPase (ATP7A) in Menkes syndrome
questions.exp: Trichothiodystrophy (TTD) is a rare autosomal recessive DNA repair/transcription disorder with mutations in TFIIH complex genes (ERCC2/XPD, ERCC3/XPB, GTF2H5/TTDA). The tiger-tail pattern on polarizing light microscopy and the syndromic features (photosensitivity, intellectual impairment, ichthyosis) are pathognomonic for TTD, reflecting a profound sulfur-containing amino acid deficiency.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: A TIGER prowls through a GOTHIC CATHEDRAL (TFIIH complex)—its STRIPES (tiger-tail banding) glow under UV light, revealing SULFUR DEFICIENCY. The tiger cannot REPAIR or TRANSCRIBE DNA, trapped in a PHOTOSENSITIVE DUNGEON.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with a 6-month history of asymptomatic, small red-brown papules on his trunk and proximal arms. Each papule is capped with a tightly adherent scale that, when gently scraped away, reveals a shining brown surface beneath. Histology shows superficial perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with vacuolar interface dermatitis and focal parakeratosis. Which of the following best explains the cellular mechanism driving this condition?
opts: CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell-mediated response with massive epidermal necrosis
CD4+ helper T-cell-mediated hypersensitivity response, with some regulatory T-cells expressing FoxP3
Humoral autoimmune response with pathogenic anti-basement membrane IgG autoantibodies
Neutrophil-driven innate immune response with polymorphous infiltration
questions.exp: Pityriasis lichenoides chronica (PLC) is driven by cellular immunity, specifically CD4+ helper T-cells rather than CD8+ cytotoxic cells seen in PLEVA. The presence of FoxP3+ regulatory T-cells accounts for the more indolent, chronic nature. PLC is not an autoantibody-mediated disease and is theorized to be triggered by exogenous antigens (infectious agents or drugs), not self-antigens.

questions.q: A 16-year-old girl with rubella develops joint pain affecting her fingers, wrists, and knees that persists for several weeks. Which population group shows the strongest predilection for this arthritic complication of rubella?
opts: Postpubertal males across all ethnicities
Prepubertal children regardless of sex
Postpubertal females, occurring in up to 70% of cases
Individuals with HLA-B27 allele exclusively
questions.exp: Postpubertal females frequently (up to 70%) develop arthralgias and arthritis affecting the fingers, wrists, and knees during classic rubella infection, with these symptoms potentially persisting for weeks. This is a well-documented female predilection not seen in prepubertal children or males.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with poorly defined, round hypopigmented macules with fine powdery scale on his cheeks that failed to tan during summer. Histology shows mild spongiosis, hyperkeratosis, and early follicular plugging with atrophic sebaceous glands. Which pathophysiological mechanism best explains the hypopigmentation in this case?
opts: Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes mediated by anti-melanocyte antibodies
Low-grade eczematous dermatitis disrupting melanosome transfer from melanocytes to keratinocytes, potentially worsened by tyrosinase inhibition from Malassezia metabolites or low serum copper
Complete loss of dermal melanin due to deep pigmentary incontinence and phagocytosis by macrophages
Genetic mutation in the FLG gene causing primary epidermal barrier dysfunction with secondary melanin loss
questions.exp: Pityriasis alba is fundamentally a post-inflammatory hypopigmentation arising from low-grade localized eczema that disrupts melanosome transfer. The condition is not autoimmune and does not involve pathogenic autoantibodies or target autoantigens. Dicarboxylic acids from Malassezia or low serum copper may inhibit tyrosinase, the enzyme critical for melanin synthesis.

questions.q: A 2-year-old boy with facial dysmorphism, congenital heart defects, and widespread cutaneous papillomas is brought to your clinic. His parents are unaffected. Genetic testing reveals a de novo mutation in the Ras/MAPK signaling pathway. Which of the following best explains the pathophysiological basis of this child's condition?
opts: Autoimmune-mediated destruction of ectodermal tissues with pathogenic IgG antibodies
Aberrant activation of the Ras/mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) intracellular signaling cascade
HLA-associated immune complex deposition in the basement membrane zone
Deficiency of natural killer cell function with secondary opportunistic infection
questions.exp: Cardio-facio-cutaneous syndrome and related RASopathies are primary inherited genetic developmental disorders caused by de novo germ-line mutations that aberrantly activate the Ras/MAPK intracellular signaling pathway, NOT autoimmune or HLA-associated diseases. The condition affects ectodermal and mesodermal structures including the epidermis, hair follicles, cardiovascular system, and craniofacial bones.

questions.q: A 28-year-old primigravida develops a rapidly enlarging, friable red nodule on her anterior maxillary gingiva during the first trimester of pregnancy. She is counselled about the natural history of this lesion. Which of the following statements regarding the postpartum course is most accurate?
opts: Complete spontaneous regression occurs in all cases within 3 months postpartum
Partial or complete spontaneous regression often occurs in the postpartum period
The lesion invariably persists unchanged throughout the postpartum period
Spontaneous regression is rare and excision is mandatory in all pregnant patients
questions.exp: Pregnancy-related pyogenic granulomas (granuloma gravidarum) often arise on gingiva during the first half of pregnancy and are hormonally-driven. Characteristically, these lesions undergo partial or complete spontaneous regression in the postpartum period, reflecting withdrawal of pregnancy hormones, though not all cases regress completely.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: A PREGNANT QUEEN in the castle courtyard grows a FRIABLE RED TUMOR on her gums—but when she delivers the BABY, her hormones shift and the tumor SHRINKS away like magic, vanishing into the postpartum mist!

questions.q: A 16-year-old girl presents with extensive hypopigmented patches exceeding 2 cm in diameter distributed over her trunk and limbs with a fine white scale. Which of the following best distinguishes this presentation from classic childhood pityriasis alba?
opts: Classic PA affects teenagers and young adults with female preponderance; extensive PA is limited to young children with facial involvement
Extensive PA presents with larger lesions (>2 cm) in teenagers and young adults with female preponderance, whereas classic PA is primarily a childhood facial condition with smaller lesions
Extensive PA involves autoimmune mechanisms; classic PA is purely eczematous
Extensive PA shows complete sebaceous gland loss histologically; classic PA shows only follicular plugging
questions.exp: The extensive (generalized) variant of pityriasis alba is distinguished by larger lesions (typically >2 cm), widespread trunk and limb involvement, and a predilection for teenagers and young adults with female preponderance. Classic PA favors the face in children with lesions 0.5–3 cm in diameter. Both variants share the same eczematous pathophysiology.

questions.q: A 7-year-old girl of African descent presents with short, dull, brittle hair that breaks easily and fails to grow beyond shoulder length. Her mother reports using chemical relaxers monthly since age 3. Microscopic examination reveals focal loss of the cuticular layer with exposed, frayed cortical fibers forming transverse fractures that resemble opposing paintbrushes. Which hair shaft disorder best explains these findings?
opts: Trichothiodystrophy (TTD) with tiger-tail banding pattern
Trichorrhexis nodosa (TN) with nodal fragility
Trichorrhexis invaginata presenting as bamboo hair
Trichoschisis from cysteine deficiency
questions.exp: Trichorrhexis nodosa is the most common hair shaft defect characterized by grayish-white nodules and transverse fracturing. The paintbrush/broomstick appearance is pathognomonic. In individuals of African descent, acquired proximal TN is specifically linked to chemical relaxers and heat trauma, matching this clinical presentation perfectly.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: Imagine an African Queen's hair RELAXER turning her castle's PAINT BRUSHES into NODULAR MOPS—each BRUSH HEAD (node) shedding frayed bristles at a TRANSVERSE CUT.

questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes MPS Type I from MPS Type II regarding inheritance pattern and causative enzyme deficiency?
opts: MPS I is X-linked recessive caused by iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency; MPS II is autosomal recessive caused by alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency
MPS I is autosomal recessive caused by alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency; MPS II is X-linked recessive caused by iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency
Both are autosomal recessive but differ in the location of enzyme deficiency within the lysosome
MPS I is X-linked dominant; MPS II is X-linked recessive, both affecting enzyme function in the Golgi apparatus
questions.exp: MPS Type I (Hurler Syndrome) is autosomal recessive with mutations in the IDUA gene causing alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency. MPS Type II (Hunter Syndrome) is the only MPS with X-linked recessive inheritance, caused by IDS gene mutations encoding iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency. This critical genetic distinction determines inheritance patterns and clinical presentation severity.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: An AUTOSOMAL HURLER runs through one door (both parents carry key) while the X-LINKED HUNTER sneaks through the male-only passage—only sons inherit the curse from mother's corridor.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with fever, irritability, and a rapidly progressive scarlatiniform rash starting on the face and spreading to intertriginous areas. Within 48 hours, large flaccid bullae develop that rupture easily, leaving moist denuded areas. Intraorally, the mucous membranes appear completely normal. Which molecular mechanism explains the mucosal sparing observed in this case of generalized SSSS?
opts: Staphylococcal exfoliative toxins preferentially target Desmoglein-3, which is absent from mucous membranes
Mucous membranes rely primarily on Desmoglein-3 for cellular adhesion, which is unaffected by staphylococcal exfoliative toxins
Saliva contains high concentrations of toxin-neutralizing antibodies that protect the oral mucosa
The stratum granulosum is thicker in mucosal epithelium, preventing toxin penetration
questions.exp:
Staphylococcal exfoliative toxins (ETA and ETB) specifically cleave Desmoglein-1 (Dsg1) in the superficial epidermis, but mucous membranes primarily utilize Desmoglein-3 for cell-to-cell adhesion. Since Dsg3 is not a substrate for these toxins, mucosal integrity is preserved despite widespread cutaneous involvement.
🏰 Palace: Picture a CASTLE with two GATES—Gate 1 (Dsg1) is SMASHED by the invading STAPHYLOCOCCUS army, but Gate 3 (Dsg3) in the THRONE ROOM (mucosa) remains LOCKED and UNTOUCHED by their weapons.

questions.q: A 6-year-old boy presents with ivory-white papules and nodules coalescing into a reticular 'pebbly' pattern on his back and scapulae. He also has Mongolian blue spots, generalized hirsutism, and coarse facial features but notably clear corneas. Which enzyme deficiency is responsible for his condition?
opts: Alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency
Iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency
Arylsulfatase A deficiency
Galactocerebrosidase deficiency
questions.exp: The pathognomonic ivory-white papules forming a pebbly pattern on the back, combined with clear corneas and X-linked inheritance affecting males, is characteristic of MPS Type II (Hunter Syndrome). The disease results from iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency encoded by the IDS gene, leading to dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate accumulation. Unlike MPS Type I (Hurler Syndrome), Hunter syndrome lacks corneal clouding and presents the distinctive pebbly skin pattern.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a HUNTED DEER with IVORY PEBBLY BACK fleeing through castle corridors with CLEAR EYES—it escapes the corneal CLOUD that traps the HURLER in the courtyard.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with a bizarre, angular patch of alopecia on the frontoparietal scalp. His mother reports he pulls his hair unconsciously while watching television. The child denies any distress and the hair loss is limited to one area. Which of the following best describes the expected prognosis and pathomechanism?
opts: Chronic condition with high psychiatric comorbidity; mediated by perifollicular lymphocytic infiltration
Generally benign and self-limiting habit; mechanical trauma to terminal hair shafts and anagen bulbs without significant inflammation
Progressive scarring alopecia; autoimmune attack on hair follicle autoantigens with HLA-B27 association
Acute inflammatory disorder requiring immediate immunosuppressive therapy; associated with elevated tissue autoantibodies
questions.exp: Childhood trichotillomania is typically an unconscious, self-soothing habit with excellent prognosis. The pathomechanism is purely mechanical trauma (trichoclasis and trichomalacia) without immune involvement, distinguishing it from autoimmune alopecias like alopecia areata, which show perifollicular inflammation and lack HLA associations in TTM.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: A young KNIGHT (7yo) mindlessly PLUCKS GRASS (mechanical trauma, anagen bulbs) in the castle courtyard while WATCHING A TOURNAMENT (TV), leaving a ZIGZAG MOAT (bizarre angular patch)—the castle heals itself perfectly because it's just BRANCH-BREAKING, not an INVADING ARMY (no inflammation, no immune cells).

questions.q: According to modern medical consensus, what is the current status of 4th disease (Filatov-Dukes disease) as a distinct diagnostic entity?
opts: It is recognized as a distinct disease caused by a specific viral pathogen
It is widely considered an obsolete medical diagnosis not recognized as an independent disease entity
It is classified as a variant of measles with characteristic strawberry tongue
It is confirmed as a staphylococcal infection with severe pharyngitis and systemic toxicity
questions.exp: Modern medicine and microbiology do not recognize 4th disease as a distinct, independent disease entity or a separate causative pathogen. The condition is now understood to represent misdiagnosis or overlap of other known exanthems that were not fully defined at the turn of the 20th century.

questions.q: A neonate develops a localized infection at the umbilical stump with subsequent disseminated blistering and skin desquamation affecting the face, neck, axillae, and gluteal cleft. Which staphylococcal exfoliative toxin is most frequently implicated in this generalized presentation, and what is its genetic location?
opts: Exfoliative toxin A (ETA), encoded on a large plasmid
Exfoliative toxin B (ETB), encoded on a large plasmid
Exfoliative toxin A (ETA), chromosomally encoded
Exfoliative toxin B (ETB), chromosomally encoded
questions.exp:
While both ETA and ETB target Desmoglein-1, ETB is more frequently associated with generalized SSSS. ETB is encoded on a large plasmid, whereas ETA is chromosomally encoded and more commonly isolated from localized bullous impetigo.
🏰 Palace: Imagine PLASMID-shaped PEARLS (ETB = Plasmid-encoded Toxin B) rolling through a GENERALIZED BALLROOM causing WIDESPREAD DESTRUCTION, while the CHROMOSOME-bound ARMOR (ETA) stays LOCAL in a small courtyard.

questions.q: A 6-month-old infant with a giant congenital melanocytic nevus (58 cm × 62 cm across the trunk) undergoes dermoscopy and initial dermato-histopathology. Which genetic mutation is most likely detected, and what is the pathognomonic histological finding in the dermis?
opts: BRAF V600E mutation; nevomelanocytes arranged in palisaded clusters at the dermal-epidermal junction only
NRAS codon 61 mutation; nevomelanocytes in 'Indian file' single-file arrays infiltrating between collagen bundles and around skin appendages/vessels
KIT mutation; spindle-shaped melanocytes limited to the superficial dermis with sparse hair follicle involvement
TP53 mutation; atypical melanocytes with prominent nuclear pleomorphism confined to the epidermis
questions.exp: NRAS mutations at codon 61 are detected in 70–80% of CMNs and are highly associated with large and giant CMNs. The pathognomonic histological feature is the 'Indian file' single-file arrangement of nevomelanocytes splaying between collagen bundles and heavily infiltrating the adventitia of skin adnexa, blood vessels, and nerves throughout the dermis and subcutis. BRAF mutations are more common in smaller CMNs; KIT and TP53 are not characteristic of CMN.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: An NRAS GIANT in a BATHING TUB (giant CMN) walks down a SINGLE-FILE INDIAN LINE (Indian file) through the COLLAGEN CASTLE HALLWAY, tickling HAIR FOLLICLES and BLOOD VESSELS as he marches.

questions.q: A 4-year-old girl presents with multiple profuse dark brown macules (lentigines) across her face and trunk, widely spaced eyes, a cardiac murmur consistent with pulmonary stenosis, growth retardation, and sensorineural hearing loss. Her parents report normal development in both maternal and paternal family members. Which RASopathy diagnosis best fits this clinical presentation?
opts: Cardio-facio-cutaneous syndrome with primary facial dysmorphism
Costello syndrome presenting with diffuse cutaneous papillomas
LEOPARD syndrome
Noonan syndrome with isolated pulmonic stenosis
questions.exp: LEOPARD syndrome is a distinctive RASopathy defined by the classic eponymous acronym: Lentigines, ECG abnormalities, Ocular hypertelorism, Pulmonary stenosis, Abnormalities of genitalia, Retardation of growth, and Deafness (sensorineural). This patient demonstrates the characteristic triad of lentigines, ocular hypertelorism, pulmonary stenosis, growth retardation, and sensorineural hearing loss.

questions.q: Which of the following findings is pathognomonic for sclerema neonatorum on histopathological examination?
opts: Vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis of subcutaneous blood vessels accompanied by dense neutrophilic infiltration
Doubly refractile, needle-shaped clefts arranged radially within adipocytes with marked absence of inflammation
Septal panniculitis with CD8+ lymphocytic infiltration and adipocyte apoptosis
Sclerotic fibrosis of subcutaneous tissue with obliteration of fat lobules and granuloma formation
questions.exp: The pathognomonic histological feature of sclerema neonatorum is the presence of doubly refractile, needle-shaped clefts arranged radially within adipocytes, representing dissolved triglyceride crystals. Critically, there is a striking absence of inflammation or only very sparse inflammatory infiltrate, which distinguishes it from other panniculitides and reflects its non-inflammatory, purely crystallization-based pathogenesis.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 4] Sclerema neonatorum vs Subcutaneous fat necrosis of newborn
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Under the microscope's magnifying glass, imagine GLITTERING STAR-SHAPED NEEDLES (doubly refractile crystals) radiating like a SILENT SNOWSTORM inside the fat cells—NO ANGRY GUARDS (inflammation) watching, just pure crystalline devastation in an eerily QUIET, EMPTY CASTLE HALL.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with a rapidly growing, bright red pedunculated nodule on his finger that bleeds easily with minor trauma. Histopathology shows lobular proliferations of capillary endothelial cells in the superficial dermis with an epithelial collarette at the periphery. According to ISSVA classification, how should this lesion be categorized?
opts: Benign vascular tumour
Vascular malformation
Granulomatous inflammatory condition
Infectious vascular proliferation
questions.exp: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary haemangioma) is classified by ISSVA strictly under 'Benign Vascular Tumours,' distinguishing it definitively from vascular malformations. Despite its historical name, it is not a true granuloma (lacking granulomatous architecture) nor pyogenic (not infection-driven), making it a reactive vascular hyperplasia.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture ISSVA's castle throne room where BENIGN VASCULAR TUMOURS sit on the royal chair—the granuloma was always invited to the wrong party (pyogenic/granuloma), but ISSVA finally gave it the correct seat at the vascular tumour banquet!

questions.q: A 3-week-old term male infant presents with multiple small erythematous papules and pustules on the cheeks, forehead, and chin. The mother is concerned about permanent scarring. Which of the following findings would be most consistent with neonatal acne (neonatal cephalic pustulosis)?
opts: Presence of prominent open and closed comedones on histology
Absence of true comedones with non-comedonal pustular inflammatory eruption
Deep suppurative nodules with pitted scarring in 50% of cases
Elevated levels of luteinizing hormone stimulating testicular testosterone
questions.exp: Neonatal acne characteristically lacks true comedones and presents as a non-comedonal pustular inflammatory eruption driven by Malassezia species colonization and transient neonatal androgens. The lesions resolve spontaneously within 1–3 months without scarring, distinguishing it from infantile acne which does present with comedones and causes pitted scarring in up to 50% of cases.

questions.q: A 16-year-old girl with major depression and anxiety presents with scalp hair reduced to coarse stubble. She consciously identifies specific hairs as feeling 'abnormal' and engages in ritualized removal. She denies her behaviour due to profound shame. Which of the following statements about her condition is INCORRECT?
opts: Her presentation represents the adolescent/adult chronic psychiatric type with focused pulling behaviour
Her psychiatric comorbidities show a female predominance of 4:1 to 10:1 in this age group compared to males
Her condition is mediated by perifollicular and peribulbar lymphocytic infiltration, similar to alopecia areata
Her hair loss results from mechanical fracturing of hair shafts and structural distortion of the hair bulb
questions.exp: Trichotillomania is a mechanical, body-focused repetitive behaviour disorder with NO immune component; there is a strict absence of significant perifollicular or peribulbar inflammation, distinguishing it from autoimmune alopecias. All other statements accurately describe adolescent TTM with chronic psychiatric comorbidity.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: A teenage PRINCESS (16yo, female predominance) sits in the TOWER (depression/anxiety) PLUCKING THREADS (mechanical trauma) from her GOWN (conscious focused pulling), denying the TRUTH (shame). She studies a MIRROR showing NO ANGRY RED GUARDS at the hair follicles (NO perifollicular inflammation—it's mechanical, not immune).

questions.q: A 4-year-old girl is found to have a mixture of comedones and inflammatory papules on her face during a routine pediatric examination. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
opts: Reassure parents that mid-childhood acne is a normal variant that will self-resolve with topical retinoids
Initiate oral antibiotics and benzoyl peroxide therapy for the inflammatory lesions
Perform immediate endocrine evaluation to rule out hyperandrogenism, premature adrenarche, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, or androgen-secreting tumor
Prescribe isotretinoin given the high risk of severe adolescent acne in this age group
questions.exp: Mid-childhood acne (ages 1–7 years) is extremely rare and represents a major clinical red flag because androgen production should be quiescent during this period. The presence of acne mandates immediate endocrine evaluation to exclude serious pathology such as hyperandrogenism or adrenal/gonadal tumors.

questions.q: Which of the following clinical features historically distinguished Filatov-Dukes disease from classic scarlet fever (2nd disease)?
opts: Presence of strawberry tongue and severe exudative pharyngitis
Absence of severe pharyngitis and absence of strawberry tongue despite scarlatiniform rash
High fever with rapid onset and diffuse lymphadenopathy
Vesicular exanthem with bullae formation
questions.exp: Dukes described a mild febrile illness with a scarlatiniform rash that lacked the severe systemic toxicity, extreme high fevers, severe exudative pharyngitis, and the pathognomonic strawberry tongue characteristic of classic scarlet fever. This presentation is now understood to match staphylococcal scarlatiniform erythroderma caused by enterotoxin-producing S. aureus acting as a superantigen.

questions.q: A neonate born at 36 hours of life is encased in a shiny, taut, translucent membrane that subsequently sheds over several weeks, revealing persistent generalized erythroderma with fine, white, feathery scales. Ectropion and palmoplantar keratoderma are noted. Histopathology shows non-specific psoriasiform acanthosis and orthokeratotic hyperkeratosis without keratin clumping. What is the inheritance pattern and primary pathophysiological defect of this condition?
opts: Autosomal dominant inheritance; structural keratin mutations in spinous layer
Autosomal recessive inheritance; defective lipid processing and stratum corneum transport
Autosomal recessive inheritance; unregulated protease activity in stratum corneum
X-linked recessive inheritance; defective barrier protein synthesis
questions.exp: Congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma (non-bullous CIEE) presents with a collodion membrane at birth, followed by persistent erythroderma and fine scales. It is autosomal recessive and involves defects in lipid processing genes (ALOX12B, ALOXE3, NIPAL4, PNPLA1, CERS3, TGM1) affecting stratum corneum function. The absence of keratin clumping on histology distinguishes it from epidermolytic ichthyosis (which is autosomal dominant).
questions.memory_aid: 🏰 Palace: A COCOON CASTLE (collodion membrane) wraps the newborn princess—when it SHEDS, she emerges into a LIPID-DEFICIENT WASTELAND (ARCI genes). Her EYEBALLS TURN OUT (ectropion) and her PALMS HARDEN (palmoplantar)—recessive damage to the LIPID BRICK WALL, not the keratin skeleton.
